questions.stem: Consider a 2-bit saturating up/down counter that performs the saturating up count when the input $P$ is 0, and the saturating down count when $P$ is 1. The Next State table of the counter is as shown. The counter is built as a synchronous sequential circuit using D flip-flops. Which one of the following options corresponds to the expressions for the inputs of the D flip-flops, $D_1$ and $D_0$?

solutionDiagram.alt: Two K-maps over P and Q1Q0 with the grouped ones that give D1 and D0

steps.title: What a D flip-flop needs, and what the table gives
steps.body: A D flip-flop copies its input $D$ into its output $Q$ at every clock edge, so $Q^+ = D$: the value that must be present at $D$ is simply the next-state value we want. A saturating counter is one that stops at its end value instead of wrapping: counting up it stays at 11, counting down it stays at 00. The table already lists the next state $Q_1^+Q_0^+$ for every combination of the input $P$ and the present state $Q_1Q_0$. So the rule that decides the question is: $D_1$ is the function that equals the column $Q_1^+$, and $D_0$ is the function that equals the column $Q_0^+$, row by row, over all 8 rows.

steps.title: Read the two columns as functions of P, Q1, Q0
steps.body: Group the rows by $P$. For $P=0$ (count up) the column $Q_1^+$ reads 0, 1, 1, 1 for $Q_1Q_0 = 00, 01, 10, 11$; for $P=1$ (count down) it reads 0, 0, 0, 1. The column $Q_0^+$ reads 1, 0, 1, 1 for $P=0$ and 0, 0, 1, 0 for $P=1$, again for $Q_1Q_0 = 00, 01, 10, 11$.

steps.title: Minimise D1 with a K-map
steps.body: On the K-map of $D_1$ the ones are: for $P=0$ the cells $Q_1Q_0=01, 11, 10$, and for $P=1$ the single cell $Q_1Q_0=11$. Group the pair $\overline{P}Q_1$ (cells 11 and 10 with $P=0$), the pair $\overline{P}Q_0$ (cells 01 and 11 with $P=0$) and the pair $Q_1Q_0$ (cell 11 with both values of $P$). Every 1 is covered and no 0 is.

steps.title: Minimise D0 the same way
steps.body: The ones of $D_0$ are: for $P=0$ the cells 00, 11, 10, and for $P=1$ the cell 10. Group $\overline{P}\,\overline{Q_0}$ (cells 00 and 10 with $P=0$, which touch across the edge of the map), $\overline{P}Q_1$ (cells 11 and 10 with $P=0$) and $Q_1\overline{Q_0}$ (cell 10 with both values of $P$).

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: Option (B) has $D_1 = \overline{P}Q_1 + \overline{P}Q_0 + Q_1Q_0$ and $D_0 = \overline{P}\,\overline{Q_0} + \overline{P}Q_1 + Q_1\overline{Q_0}$, exactly the two expressions above. Each of the other three options fails on at least one row (for example the row $P=0, Q_1Q_0=00$ must give 01), so the answer is (B).

shortcut.body: Do not minimise: test one row on the options. Row $P=0$, $Q_1Q_0=00$ must give $Q_1^+Q_0^+ = 01$, so $D_1=0$ and $D_0=1$. Options A and D give $D_0=0$ and option C gives $D_1=1$ on that row; only B gives $D_1=0, D_0=1$. One row and about 30 seconds decide it. The shortcut is safe here because each wrong option fails on that single easy row; if two options survived, test a second row such as $P=1$, $Q_1Q_0=11$.

traps.text: Option A fails on the first row: with $P=0$ and $Q_1Q_0=00$ its $D_0$ is $P Q_0 + \overline{P}Q_1 + Q_1\overline{Q_0} = 0$, but the table needs $Q_0^+=1$. It uses $P$ where the up count needs $\overline{P}$.
Option C writes $\overline{P}\,\overline{Q_1}$ as the first term of $D_1$, which is 1 on the row $P=0, Q_1Q_0=00$, but the table says $Q_1^+=0$ there (the counter goes 00 to 01, not to 10).

Option D uses $P\overline{Q_1}$ and $P\overline{Q_0}$, the down-count variables, where the up-count rows need $\overline{P}$; at $P=0, Q_1Q_0=00$ it gives $D_0=0$ instead of 1. Mixing the polarity of $P$ is the common slip, since the up count is $P=0$.

recognize.clues: The words "synchronous sequential circuit using D flip-flops" together with a table of next states $Q_1^+Q_0^+$ for each $P$, $Q_1$, $Q_0$ mean the D inputs are read straight off the table and then matched to an expression.
recognize.contrast: With JK or T flip-flops you would first need the excitation table (what J, K or T must be to cause each change). With D flip-flops the input equals the next state, so no excitation table is needed.

check.body: Test a row that was not used to pick the option. For the saturating row $P=0$, $Q_1Q_0=11$ the counter must stay at 11, and for $P=1$, $Q_1Q_0=11$ it must go to 10. Substitute both rows into the chosen $D_1$ and $D_0$.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2026 Set 1 question 37
GATE 2026 CS-1 answer key, IIT Guwahati (organising institute)

hints.text: What value has to be present at a D input so that the flip-flop holds the wanted bit after the next clock edge?
A D flip-flop copies its input at the clock edge, so each D input is simply the next-state bit that the table lists for that row.
Treat the $Q_1^+$ column and the $Q_0^+$ column as two Boolean functions of the three variables $P$, $Q_1$, $Q_0$. A candidate expression is right only if it reproduces its column on all eight rows.
You do not have to minimise anything. Pick one row, read the two next-state bits from the table, and substitute that row's values of $P$, $Q_1$, $Q_0$ into each option's $D_1$ and $D_0$.

Try the row $P=1$, $Q_1Q_0=00$, where the table shows the counter staying at 00. Both $D$ inputs must be 0 there, which removes at least one option; then repeat with another row for the options that remain.

variation.stem: A 2-bit synchronous counter is built from D flip-flops and has an enable input $E$. When $E=1$ it counts up with wrap-around, 00, 01, 10, 11, 00, and when $E=0$ it holds its state. Which option gives the correct D inputs?
variation.explanation: For a D flip-flop the input is the next state. The low bit flips whenever $E=1$, so $D_0=Q_0\oplus E$. The high bit flips only when $E=1$ and $Q_0=1$ (a carry), so $D_1=Q_1\oplus E\,Q_0$. The first option flips $Q_1$ without waiting for the carry, the second can never clear a bit, and the fourth sends $Q_0$ to 0 whenever $E=0$.

questions.stem: In a 4-bit ripple counter, if the period of the waveform at the last flip-flop is 64 microseconds, then the frequency of the ripple counter in kHz is ________. (Answer in integer)

solutionDiagram.alt: Timing waveforms of a 4-bit ripple counter: each stage has twice the period of the stage before, and Q3 spans 16 clock periods

steps.title: What a ripple counter is
steps.body: A ripple counter is an asynchronous counter: only the first flip-flop receives the external clock, and the clock input of every later flip-flop is the output of the one before it. Each flip-flop is a T flip-flop with $T=1$, so it toggles once per falling edge it sees. A flip-flop that toggles once per input cycle gives an output with exactly twice the period, that is, half the frequency, of its input. The frequency of the ripple counter is the frequency of the external clock fed to the first stage.

steps.title: Each stage doubles the period
steps.body: Let the clock period be $T_{clk}$. The output of stage 1 has period $2T_{clk}$, stage 2 has $4T_{clk}$, stage 3 has $8T_{clk}$, and stage 4, the last one, has $16T_{clk} = 2^4 T_{clk}$.

steps.title: Solve for the clock and convert
steps.body: With $T_{\text{last}} = 64\ \mu\text{s}$, $T_{clk} = 64/16 = 4\ \mu\text{s}$. The frequency is $1/T_{clk} = 1/(4\times 10^{-6}\ \text{s}) = 250{,}000$ Hz $= 250$ kHz. The waveform drawing shows 16 clock periods fitting inside one period of the last output.

shortcut.body: An $n$-bit ripple counter divides the clock by $2^n$, so $f_{clk} = 2^n \times f_{\text{last}}$. Here $f_{\text{last}} = 1/64\ \mu\text{s} = 15.625$ kHz and $15.625 \times 16 = 250$ kHz. Writing it as $16/64\ \mu\text{s}$ gives the answer in one step, about 30 seconds.

traps.text: 125 comes from dividing by $2^3 = 8$ instead of $2^4 = 16$: a 4-bit counter has four toggling stages, and the last output is the fourth, not the third.
15.625 is the frequency of the last flip-flop output, $1/64\ \mu\text{s}$. The question asks for the frequency of the counter, which is the input clock, 16 times higher.
0.977 (about 1) comes from multiplying the period by 16 instead of dividing: the clock is faster than the last stage, so its period is shorter than 64 microseconds.

recognize.clues: "4-bit ripple counter" with a period quoted for the last flip-flop: the last output is the clock divided by $2^4$, so its period is $2^4$ clock periods.
recognize.contrast: This is not the maximum-frequency question for a ripple counter (dl-sequential-circuits.ripple-fmax), where the delays of the stages add up. No delay is given here, only the dividing ratio.

check.body: Run it forwards from the answer: a clock of that frequency has some period, 16 of those periods must equal the stated 64 microseconds, and dividing the clock frequency by 16 must give the frequency of the last output, whose period is 64 microseconds.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2025 Set 2 question 34
GATE 2025 CS-2 final answer key, IIT Roorkee (organising institute)

hints.text: How does the period of a flip-flop's output compare with the period of the signal that clocks it?
In a ripple counter each T flip-flop is clocked by the output of the one before it, and with $T=1$ it toggles once for every cycle of its own clock.
One toggle per input cycle means one output cycle takes two input cycles, so every stage doubles the period. The last stage's period is therefore the clock period times $2^n$ for $n$ stages.
Count the stages, form $2^n$, divide the given period of the last output by it to get the clock period, then take the reciprocal and convert to kHz.
The counter has 4 stages, so the factor is 16: the given 64 microseconds is 16 clock periods long. Divide, then invert.

variation.stem: In a 5-bit ripple counter built from T flip-flops with $T=1$, the output of the last flip-flop has a period of 160 microseconds. Find the frequency of the clock applied to the first flip-flop, in kHz. (Answer in integer)
variation.explanation: Five stages divide the clock by $2^5=32$, so one period of the last output holds 32 clock periods and the clock period is $160/32=5$ microseconds. The frequency is $1/(5\ \mu\text{s})=200$ kHz.

questions.stem: Consider a finite state machine (FSM) with one input $X$ and one output $f$, represented by the given state transition table. The minimum number of states required to realize this FSM is ________. (Answer in integer)

solutionDiagram.alt: State graph of the minimised FSM with states A,C then B,E then D,H plus F and G, with X/f labels

steps.title: Equivalent states and the refinement rule
steps.body: Two states of a machine are equivalent when, started in either, every input sequence produces the same output sequence. Equivalent states can be merged without changing the behaviour, and the smallest machine has one state per equivalence class. To find the classes, use partition refinement: first put states in the same group if their outputs agree for every input; then split a group whenever two of its states send some input into different groups; repeat until no group splits. The groups left are the classes.

steps.title: Start with the output rows
steps.body: The output pair $(f \text{ at } X=0,\ f \text{ at } X=1)$ is: A (0,0), B (0,0), C (0,0), D (1,0), E (0,0), F (1,1), G (0,1), H (1,0). The first partition is $\{A,B,C,E\}$, $\{D,H\}$, $\{F\}$, $\{G\}$.

steps.title: Split by successors
steps.body: In $\{A,B,C,E\}$ the successors (on $X=0$, $X=1$) are A: (F, B), B: (D, C), C: (F, E), E: (D, C). A and C go to F on 0 and into $\{A,B,C,E\}$ on 1; B and E go to D, which is in $\{D,H\}$, on 0. So the group splits into $\{A,C\}$ and $\{B,E\}$. In $\{D,H\}$ both states go to (G, A), so it does not split.

steps.title: Check that nothing splits further
steps.body: Now the partition is $\{A,C\}$, $\{B,E\}$, $\{D,H\}$, $\{F\}$, $\{G\}$. A goes to (F, B) and C to (F, E): B and E are in the same group, so A and C still agree. B and E both go to (D, C), D and H both go to (G, A). No group splits, so these five groups are the equivalence classes, and the minimal FSM has 5 states (see the drawing of the merged machine).

shortcut.body: Scan the table for two rows that are identical in outputs and next states. D and H both read (G, A) with outputs (1, 0), and B and E both read (D, C) with outputs (0, 0): merge those pairs at once, since identical rows are equivalent. Then A and C differ only in B versus E, which you just merged, so merge A and C. Nothing else matches: 8 - 3 = 5. Unsafe if you stop after the first obvious pairs, so always finish with the cascade check.

traps.text: 8 means no states were merged: the table looks irregular, and a candidate writes the table size without merging anything, or compares only the outputs and never the successors, so no pair is ever recognised as equivalent.
6 comes from merging only the identical-row pairs B,E and D,H and missing that A and C become equivalent once B and E are merged; the cascade step is where this question is decided.
4 or fewer comes from merging states that merely look alike but whose output pairs differ, such as D (1, 0) with F (1, 1); states with different outputs are never equivalent.

recognize.clues: "Minimum number of states required to realize this FSM" with a complete table of next states and outputs: the task is to find the equivalence classes of the existing states.
recognize.contrast: Counting the states for a sequence detector (dl-sequential-circuits.detector-states) is design from a description. Here the machine already exists and rows of the given table are merged.

check.body: Test one merged pair on a string. Feed the input 1, 0, 0 to A and to C. Both go to the pair B, E (output 0), then to D (output 0), then to G (output 1), so both print 0, 0, 1, as equivalent states must.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2025 Set 1 question 59
GATE 2025 CS-1 final answer key, IIT Roorkee (organising institute)

hints.text: Which states can already be told apart just by watching their outputs, before looking at where they go?
Two states are equivalent when every input string gives the same output string from either one. Equivalent states can share a single state in the smallest machine.
Refine groups of states. Start from states with the same output pair, then split a group whenever two of its members send some input into different groups. Stop when no group splits.
Write each state's output pair $(f_{X=0},f_{X=1})$ and group equal pairs. Then, for every state, write which group it reaches on $X=0$ and on $X=1$.
The output pairs alone give four groups: one of four states, one of two states and two single states. Only the four-state group can still split, so test its members by where they go.

variation.stem: A Mealy machine has one input $X$ and one output $f$. Each state is given as: next state and output for $X=0$, then next state and output for $X=1$. A: B/0, C/0. B: D/0, C/1. C: B/0, F/0. D: D/1, A/0. E: F/0, A/0. F: D/1, C/0. G: D/1, A/0. No start state is given, so count all seven listed states, reachable or not. The minimum number of states required to realize this machine is ________. (Answer in integer)
variation.explanation: D and G have the same output pair and the same successors (D on 0, A on 1), so they merge. The other states split already on outputs or on successors: A, C and E share the output pair (0,0) but A goes to C on 1, C goes to F on 1 and E goes to A on 1, and C, A, F are pairwise different. That leaves 7 - 1 = 6 states.

questions.stem: Consider the given sequential circuit designed using D-Flip-flops. The circuit is initialized with some value (initial state). The number of distinct states the circuit will go through before returning back to the initial state is _________ . (Answer in integer)
questions.figure: Four D flip-flops D0, D1, D2, D3 share one clock CLK. The Q output of D0 drives the D input of D1, Q of D1 drives D of D2, and Q of D2 drives D of D3. The complemented output of D3 (the Q-bar pin of D3) drives the D input of D0, closing the loop.

diagram.alt: Four D flip-flops in a row on one clock, with the complemented output of the last wired back to the first D input

solutionDiagram.alt: Ring of the eight states 0000, 1000, 1100, 1110, 1111, 0111, 0011, 0001 of the four-bit Johnson counter

steps.title: Shift register and the Johnson feedback
steps.body: A shift register is a row of D flip-flops on one clock where the D input of each flip-flop is the Q output of its left neighbour, so at every clock edge each bit moves one place to the right. The leftmost flip-flop needs a bit from outside; in a ring counter it takes the last output $Q_3$, and in a Johnson (twisted-ring) counter it takes the complement $\overline{Q_3}$. For an $n$-bit Johnson counter the sequence of states starting from all zeros has $2n$ distinct states: $n$ clocks fill the register with 1s, and $n$ more clocks fill it with 0s again.

steps.title: Read the circuit
steps.body: Here $D_1 = Q_0$, $D_2 = Q_1$, $D_3 = Q_2$ and $D_0 = \overline{Q_3}$. The next state is therefore $(Q_0^+, Q_1^+, Q_2^+, Q_3^+) = (\overline{Q_3}, Q_0, Q_1, Q_2)$, a right shift with the inverted last bit entering at the left.

steps.title: Run it from 0000
steps.body: 0000 goes to 1000, then 1100, 1110, 1111, 0111, 0011, 0001, and the eighth clock returns to 0000. That is 8 different states in one cycle, shown in the ring drawing. Another start state, such as 0100, lies on a second cycle of its own, which also has 8 states: the 16 patterns split into two cycles of 8, so every start gives the same count.

steps.title: Interpret the count
steps.body: The circuit repeats after 8 clocks. The count asked for is 8 if the starting state is counted among the states the circuit goes through, or 7 if only the other states are counted. The official key accepts both, 7 and 8, and 8 is the standard answer: a Johnson counter of $n$ bits has $2n$ states.

shortcut.body: Recognise the pattern: a shift register with the inverted last output fed to the first input is a Johnson counter, modulus $2n = 8$. Answer 8 in under a minute without simulating. Unsafe only if the feedback is $Q_3$ without the inversion: that is a ring counter with only $n=4$ states in the cycle starting at 1000.

traps.text: 16 comes from treating the four flip-flops as a binary counter with $2^4$ states. The circuit is a shift register with feedback, and any start state sees only 8 of the 16 patterns.
4 is the length of a ring counter, where the feedback is $Q_3$ itself. The complement in the feedback doubles the cycle length to 8.
15 comes from the maximum-length cycle of a linear feedback shift register with an XOR in the feedback; here the feedback is a single inverter, not an XOR.

recognize.clues: Four D flip-flops on one clock, each D fed by the Q of its neighbour, and the complemented output of the last stage returning to the first D input: a shift register with inverted feedback.
recognize.contrast: A plain ring counter feeds back $Q_3$ itself and visits only as many states as it has flip-flops. The inversion on the feedback wire is what separates the two.

check.body: Start from a different state, 0100, and run the same rule. The states are 0100, 1010, 1101, 0110, 1011, 0101, 0010, 1001 and then 0100 again, so this cycle has the same length, and the two cycles together cover all 16 patterns.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2025 Set 1 question 60
GATE 2025 CS-1 final answer key, IIT Roorkee (organising institute)

hints.text: Write the next-state equation of each flip-flop from the wiring. What does the first flip-flop receive?
In a row of D flip-flops on one clock, each bit moves one place along at every edge, and the first flip-flop takes whatever the feedback supplies.

The feedback decides the cycle length. Returning the last bit unchanged gives a ring counter, returning its complement gives a twisted-ring (Johnson) counter, and the two cycles have different lengths.
Take 0000 as the start, shift right with the inverted last bit entering on the left, and list each new state until 0000 comes back. Note whether your count includes the start state.
From 0000 the first clock gives 1000 and the second gives 1100. Continue the same rule from there.

variation.stem: Five D flip-flops $F_0,\ldots,F_4$ share one clock. The input of $F_i$ is $Q_{i-1}$ for $i=1,\ldots,4$, and the input of $F_0$ is $\overline{Q_4}$. The circuit starts in 00000. Counting the starting state, how many distinct states does it pass through before it first returns to 00000? (Answer in integer)
variation.explanation: This is a 5-bit Johnson counter. Starting from 00000, five clocks fill the register with 1s (10000, 11000, 11100, 11110, 11111) and five more empty it again (01111, 00111, 00011, 00001, 00000). The cycle holds $2\times5=10$ distinct states.

questions.stem: The output of a 2-input multiplexer is connected back to one of its inputs as shown in the figure. Match the functional equivalence of this circuit to one of the following options.
questions.figure: A 2-to-1 multiplexer with data inputs labelled 0 and 1, a select input S, and one output Q. Input 1 comes from an external signal, S comes from an external signal, and the output Q is taken out and also wired back to data input 0.

diagram.alt: A 2-input multiplexer whose output Q is wired back to its data input 0, with input 1 and select S as the external inputs

solutionDiagram.alt: Timing of the multiplexer loop: Q copies D while S is 1 and holds while S is 0

steps.title: Combinational versus sequential, latch versus flip-flop
steps.body: A combinational circuit has outputs that depend only on the present inputs. A sequential circuit feeds its own output back, so the output also depends on stored history. A latch is a level-sensitive storage element: while its enable is active its output follows its data input (it is transparent), and when the enable is inactive it holds. A flip-flop is edge-sensitive: it samples its data input only at one clock edge. The rule that decides the question is to write the output equation, then see whether the circuit holds a bit and whether it acts on a level or an edge.

steps.title: Write the multiplexer with its feedback
steps.body: A 2-to-1 multiplexer with select $S$ outputs input 0 when $S=0$ and input 1 when $S=1$. Here input 0 is the output $Q$ itself and input 1 is the external signal $D$.

steps.title: Read the two cases
steps.body: If $S=0$, then $Q = Q$: the output feeds itself and keeps its last value, so the circuit stores a bit. If $S=1$, then $Q = D$: the output follows $D$ for as long as $S$ stays 1, and any change of $D$ during that time passes straight through. So $S$ acts as an enable, the circuit is transparent while $S=1$ and holds while $S=0$. That is a D latch (the timing drawing shows $Q$ copying $D$ only inside the $S=1$ windows). Answer: (B).

shortcut.body: Substitute the two values of $S$ in the multiplexer: one gives "hold", the other gives "copy $D$". Hold plus copy is memory, and since there is no clock edge but a level, it is a latch. About 30 seconds. Memorise: a mux with its output fed back to one data input is a D latch.

traps.text: D flip-flop is tempting because both store a bit, but a flip-flop samples only at a clock edge. Here $Q$ follows $D$ during the entire time $S=1$, which is level-sensitive behaviour.
A half-adder has two outputs, sum and carry, and no feedback or memory; this circuit has a single output that depends on its own previous value.
A demultiplexer routes one input to one of several outputs and is combinational; the circuit here has one output and a feedback loop that stores a value.

recognize.clues: The multiplexer output $Q$ returns to its own data input 0: with the select on that input the output keeps itself, so a bit is stored, and with the select on the other input it follows the external signal.
recognize.contrast: A D flip-flop needs a clock edge, or two latches in series. Here the select acts as a level enable and no clock or edge appears in the figure.

check.body: Run a short test. Hold the select high and toggle the data input up and down twice: $Q$ follows every change inside that window, which an edge-triggered element would not do. Then drop the select and change the data input again: $Q$ stays where it was.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2023 question 21
GATE 2023 CS answer key, IIT Kanpur (organising institute, PDF author IITK_GATE), IIT Guwahati archive copy

hints.text: Set the select line to each of its two values in turn. What does the output equal in each case?
A circuit whose output feeds back into its own input can remember a value, so it is sequential rather than combinational.
Memory elements differ in when they react. A level-sensitive element follows its data input for as long as it is enabled, while an edge-triggered one samples only at a clock edge.
Write $Q$ in terms of $S$, the external input and the old $Q$. Then say, for each value of $S$, whether $Q$ keeps its old value or follows the external input.

variation.stem: A 2-input multiplexer has an external signal $D$ on data input 0, its own output $Q$ fed back to data input 1, and an external select $S$. Which element does this circuit behave as?
options: D latch that is transparent while $S=0$ and holds while $S=1$
D latch that is transparent while $S=1$ and holds while $S=0$
D flip-flop that samples $D$ on the falling edge of $S$
Combinational circuit with $Q=D$ for both values of $S$
variation.explanation: The multiplexer gives $Q=D$ when $S=0$ and $Q=Q$ (the old value) when $S=1$. So $Q$ follows $D$ while $S=0$ and holds while $S=1$: a level-controlled latch with an active-low enable. The second option has the enable the wrong way round, and nothing here reacts only at an edge.

questions.stem: Consider a sequential digital circuit consisting of T flip-flops and D flip-flops as shown in the figure. CLKIN is the clock input to the circuit. At the beginning, $Q_1$, $Q_2$ and $Q_3$ have values 0, 1 and 1, respectively. Which one of the given values of $(Q_1, Q_2, Q_3)$ can NEVER be obtained with this digital circuit?
questions.figure: Three flip-flops in a row: a T flip-flop with output Q1, a D flip-flop with output Q2, and a T flip-flop with output Q3. Q1 is wired to the D input of the middle flip-flop, Q2 to the T input of the last flip-flop, and Q3 passes through an inverter whose output is wired back to the T input of the first flip-flop. All three clock pins are tied to CLKIN.

diagram.alt: Chain of T, D and T flip-flops on a common clock CLKIN, with Q3 inverted and fed back to the first T input

solutionDiagram.alt: State graph of Q1Q2Q3: a cycle of seven states through 011, with 001 isolated

steps.title: The two flip-flop rules and what synchronous means
steps.body: A D flip-flop copies its input at the clock edge: $Q^+ = D$. A T flip-flop toggles when $T=1$ and holds when $T=0$: $Q^+ = T \oplus Q$. Here all three clock pins are tied to CLKIN, so the circuit is synchronous: at each clock edge every flip-flop reads its input from the state before the edge, and all three outputs change together. A state can be reached if some run of clock edges leads to it from the start state, so the question is the set of states visited from $(0,1,1)$.

steps.title: Write the next-state equations from the wiring
steps.body: The first T flip-flop gets the inverted $Q_3$: $T_1 = \overline{Q_3}$. The D flip-flop gets $Q_1$: $D_2 = Q_1$. The last T flip-flop gets $Q_2$: $T_3 = Q_2$.
steps.tex: Q_1^{+} = Q_1 \oplus \overline{Q_3},\qquad Q_2^{+} = Q_1,\qquad Q_3^{+} = Q_3 \oplus Q_2

steps.title: Simulate from (0,1,1)
steps.body: Start (0,1,1). Clock 1: $Q_1^+ = 0\oplus 0 = 0$, $Q_2^+ = 0$, $Q_3^+ = 1\oplus 1 = 0$, giving (0,0,0). Clock 2: (1,0,0). Clock 3: (0,1,0). Clock 4: (1,0,1). Clock 5: (1,1,1). Clock 6: (1,1,0). Clock 7: (0,1,1), the start state. The machine is deterministic, so the sequence repeats forever with period 7.

steps.title: Pick the state that never appears
steps.body: The visited set is $\{011, 000, 100, 010, 101, 111, 110\}$. Option (B) 100 appears at clock 2, option (C) 101 at clock 4, option (D) 111 at clock 5. The only one of the 8 patterns missing is $(0,0,1)$, option (A), so (A) can never be obtained. The state graph shows the cycle of seven and the isolated 001.

shortcut.body: Find the predecessor of the suspect state instead of simulating. For $(0,0,1)$ to be entered, the earlier state must have $Q_1 = 0$ (since $Q_2^+ = Q_1$), then $Q_1^+ = 0$ needs $Q_3 = 1$, and $Q_3^+ = 1$ needs $Q_2 = 0$: the only predecessor is $(0,0,1)$ itself. A state whose only predecessor is itself cannot be reached from $(0,1,1)$. The full simulation takes 7 steps and about 2 minutes, so use it to confirm.

traps.text: (1,0,0) is reached at the second clock edge (011, 000, then 100). A candidate who reads the inverter at $Q_3$ wrongly, or lets $D_2$ see the new $Q_1$ instead of the old one, loses the sequence and may think it is missing.
(1,0,1) is reached at the fourth clock edge. Treating the circuit as a ripple counter, where each flip-flop is clocked by its neighbour, gives a different sequence; here all three clocks are CLKIN.
(1,1,1) is reached at the fifth clock edge. Forgetting that $T_3$ is $Q_2$ and not $Q_1$ makes this look unreachable.

recognize.clues: Mixed T and D flip-flops on one clock, a given start state, and a question about which output value can never be obtained: derive the next-state equations from the wiring and follow the deterministic sequence.
recognize.contrast: A "find the modulus" question uses the same trace but counts the cycle. Here the answer is the pattern that the cycle misses.

check.body: Test the suspect state forward. From $(0,0,1)$: $Q_1^+ = 0\oplus\overline{1} = 0$, $Q_2^+ = Q_1 = 0$, $Q_3^+ = 1\oplus 0 = 1$, so it maps to itself. A state that maps only to itself is a separate fixed point, and the seven-state cycle never leaves into it.

hints.text: What does each of the three flip-flops compute at a clock edge, and are they all updated together?
A T flip-flop gives $Q^+=T\oplus Q$ and a D flip-flop gives $Q^+=D$. With one common clock all three update at the same edge from the old values.
The circuit is deterministic, so a state can be obtained only if it lies on the path that the next-state function traces from the start state.
Write $Q_1^+$, $Q_2^+$, $Q_3^+$ in terms of $Q_1$, $Q_2$, $Q_3$ from the wiring. Compute the successor of $(0,1,1)$ and carry on until a state repeats.
The first clock takes $(0,1,1)$ to $(0,0,0)$. Continue from there and mark which of the four options appear on the path.

variation.stem: A synchronous circuit on one clock has a D flip-flop with output $Q_1$ whose D input is $\overline{Q_3}$, a D flip-flop with output $Q_2$ whose D input is $Q_1$, and a T flip-flop with output $Q_3$ whose T input is $Q_2$. It starts at $(Q_1,Q_2,Q_3)=(0,0,0)$. Which value of $(Q_1,Q_2,Q_3)$ can NEVER be obtained?
variation.explanation: The next state is $(\overline{Q_3},\,Q_1,\,Q_3\oplus Q_2)$. From 000 the sequence is 000, 100, 110, 111, 010, 101, 011 and then 000 again, seven states. The only pattern missing is 001, which is not reachable because its only predecessor is 001 itself.

questions.stem: Consider a 3-bit counter, designed using T flip-flops, as shown below: Assuming the initial state of the counter given by PQR as 000, what are the next three states?
questions.figure: Three T flip-flops with outputs P, Q and R on one clock pulse line. The T input of the P flip-flop is connected to R. The T input of the Q flip-flop is connected to the complement output P-bar. The T input of the R flip-flop is connected to the complement output Q-bar.

diagram.alt: Three T flip-flops P, Q and R with T of P tied to R, T of Q tied to the complement of P, and T of R tied to the complement of Q

solutionDiagram.alt: State graph of PQR with the cycle 000, 011, 101 and the other states that lead into it

steps.title: The T flip-flop rule and reading the wiring
steps.body: A T flip-flop holds its output when $T=0$ and toggles it when $T=1$, so $Q^+ = T \oplus Q$. All three flip-flops are clocked by the same clock pulse, so at each pulse each one uses the values that existed just before the pulse. In the figure the T input of $P$ is wired to $R$, the T input of $Q$ to $\overline{P}$ (the complement output of $P$), and the T input of $R$ to $\overline{Q}$.

steps.title: Next-state equations
steps.body: Substituting into $Q^+ = T\oplus Q$ gives the next value of each flip-flop from the present state.
steps.tex: P^{+} = P \oplus R,\qquad Q^{+} = Q \oplus \overline{P},\qquad R^{+} = R \oplus \overline{Q}

steps.title: Pulse 1 from 000
steps.body: $T_P = R = 0$, $T_Q = \overline{P} = 1$, $T_R = \overline{Q} = 1$. So $P$ holds at 0, and $Q$ and $R$ toggle to 1: the state is 011.

steps.title: Pulses 2 and 3
steps.body: From 011: $T_P = 1$, $T_Q = 1$, $T_R = 0$, so $P$ toggles to 1, $Q$ toggles to 0, $R$ holds at 1: 101. From 101: $T_P = 1$, $T_Q = 0$, $T_R = 1$, so $P$ toggles to 0, $Q$ holds at 0, $R$ toggles to 0: 000. The next three states are 011, 101, 000, which is option (A). The counter is a modulo-3 counter on 000, 011, 101; the state graph also shows the other five states and where they lead.

shortcut.body: Write $T_P, T_Q, T_R$ for the current state, toggle, and repeat three times: three one-line steps, under 2 minutes. Eliminate on the first state: with $P=Q=R=0$ only $T_Q$ and $T_R$ are 1, so the first state is 011, and that removes B and D immediately. Then only the third state separates A from C.

traps.text: Option B starts at 001. That would need only $R$ to toggle, i.e. $T_Q = 0$; but $T_Q = \overline{P} = 1$ when $P=0$, so $Q$ toggles too.
Option C reaches 111 on the third pulse. From 101 that would need $P$ to hold, but $T_P = R = 1$ there, so $P$ toggles and the state is 000.

Option D starts at 001 as well; its first two states 001 and 010 ignore the complement wiring $T_Q = \overline{P}$ and $T_R = \overline{Q}$, and only the last state 000 happens to agree with the right answer.

recognize.clues: Three T flip-flops on one pulse line, with T inputs wired from other outputs and from complements, and a request for the successive states from 000: apply $Q^+=T\oplus Q$ to all bits together.
recognize.contrast: In a ripple counter each flip-flop is clocked by the previous one and $T$ is fixed at 1. Here every clock pin shares one pulse and the T inputs depend on the state, so all bits change together.

check.body: Apply one more pulse to the claimed last state 000. It gives 011 again, the same as pulse 1, so the three states form a closed loop of length 3 that returns to the start. A wrong third state would not close the loop with the same equations.

A T flip-flop flips its output when $T=1$ and keeps it when $T=0$.
All three flip-flops share one pulse, so each decides its toggle from the old values of $P$, $Q$, $R$. Update all three together, not one after another.
Read each T input off the figure and evaluate it for the present state, apply the toggles, and repeat for each pulse.

variation.stem: A 3-bit counter is built from three T flip-flops with outputs $P$, $Q$, $R$ on one common clock. The T input of $P$ is connected to $Q$, the T input of $Q$ is connected to $R$, and the T input of $R$ is connected to $\overline{P}$. The initial state $PQR$ is 000. What are the next three states?
variation.explanation: In 000: $T_P=0$, $T_Q=0$, $T_R=1$, so only $R$ flips, giving 001. In 001: $T_P=0$, $T_Q=1$, $T_R=1$, giving 010. In 010: $T_P=1$, $T_Q=0$, $T_R=1$, giving 111. The other options come from reading $T_Q$ as $\overline{R}$, from treating the T inputs as D inputs, and from reading $T_P$ as $\overline{Q}$.

questions.stem: Suppose we want to design a synchronous circuit that processes a string of 0's and 1's. Given a string, it produces another string by replacing the first 1 in any subsequence of consecutive 1's by a 0. Consider the following example. Input sequence: 00100011000011100. Output sequence: 00000001000001100. A Mealy Machine is a state machine where both the next state and the output are functions of the present state and the current input. The above mentioned circuit can be designed as a two-state Mealy machine. The states in the Mealy machine can be represented using Boolean values 0 and 1. We denote the current state, the next state, the next incoming bit, and the output bit of the Mealy machine by the variables $s$, $t$, $b$ and $y$ respectively. Assume the initial state of the Mealy machine is 0. What are the Boolean expressions corresponding to $t$ and $y$ in terms of $s$ and $b$?

solutionDiagram.alt: Two-state Mealy machine with states s equal to 0 and 1 and edge labels b over y

steps.title: Mealy machine and what the state must remember
steps.body: In a Mealy machine the output depends on the present state and the current input, and the next state also depends on both. A machine has to remember only what the future needs. To decide the output for the current bit $b$ we need to know whether the previous bit was a 1 (then $b$, if 1, is not the first 1 of its run) or a 0 (then a 1 is the first of a run and must be replaced by 0). So the two states are: $s=0$, previous bit was 0 (or the string just started); $s=1$, previous bit was 1.

steps.title: Fill in the rule for output and next state
steps.body: Output: a 0 is copied as 0; a 1 becomes 0 if it is the first of its run ($s=0$) and stays 1 otherwise ($s=1$). So $y = 1$ only when $s=1$ and $b=1$. Next state: the new "previous bit" is the bit just read, so $t = b$ in all four cases.

steps.title: Check against the example and the options
steps.body: Run the machine on 00100011000011100 from $s=0$: each output bit is the AND of the current bit with the previous bit, giving 00000001000001100, which matches the stated output. That is option (B). Running the others on the same input gives 00000011000011100 for (A), 00010000100000010 for (C) and 00011100111100011 for (D), and none equals the example.

shortcut.body: Use the example: compare where the output is 1 in 00100011000011100 and in 00000001000001100. A 1 survives only when the bit before it is also 1, so $y = s b$ with $s$ the previous input, and the previous input is just stored: $t=b$. That settles (B) in about a minute without drawing a table. Check one extra case: input 1 then 1 must give output 0 then 1.

traps.text: Option A keeps the state at 1 forever once a 1 has been read ($t=s+b$), so every later 1 outputs 1, even the first 1 of a new run. The output for the example gets a 1 at position 7 where the target has 0.
Option C has $y = s\overline{b}$, which is 1 when the previous bit was 1 and the current bit is 0: it flags the end of a run, not the first 1 being removed, and the output is 1 at a 0 input.
Option D combines the two slips: a state that never resets, and an output that fires on a 0 after a 1. The output sequence it produces is almost the inverse of the one required.

recognize.clues: "Mealy machine" with two states, a present state $s$, an input bit $b$ and an output $y$: the output depends on $s$ and on the bit being read now, and is produced as that bit arrives.
recognize.contrast: A Moore machine's output depends on the state alone, so it cannot look at the current input and usually needs more states for the same job.

check.body: Try two short inputs from state 0. The input 1 alone must give output 0, since a lone 1 is the first of its run. The input 1, 1 must give 0 then 1, and the input 1, 0 must give 0 then 0. The chosen pair of expressions has to reproduce all three.

hints.text: What does the machine have to remember about the past in order to decide the output for the current bit?
In a Mealy machine both the output and the next state depend on the present state and the current input. Here a single state bit is enough.
Let the state bit hold exactly the fact the output needs, and nothing more. Then write the output and the next-state rule as Boolean expressions in $s$ and $b$.
Compare the input and output strings position by position. At each position where the output is 1, look at what the input bit just before it was.

variation.stem: A synchronous circuit reads a bit string and outputs 1 exactly when the current bit differs from the previous bit; the first bit is compared with an imaginary previous bit 0. It is a two-state Mealy machine with state $s$ (initial value 0), input bit $b$, next state $t$ and output $y$. For example, the input 0011010001110 gives the output 0010111001001. Which option gives $t$ and $y$?
variation.explanation: Let the state remember the previous bit, so $t=b$. The output is 1 when the previous bit and the current bit differ, so $y=s\oplus b$. Running the example from $s=0$ reproduces 0010111001001, while the other options give 0001000000110, 0011010001110 and 0000101110001.

questions.stem: Consider the sequential circuit shown in the figure, where both flip-flops used are positive edge-triggered D flip-flops. The number of states in the state transition diagram of this circuit that have a transition back to the same state on some value of "in" is _____.
questions.figure: Two positive edge-triggered D flip-flops side by side sharing one clock. The external input "in" is wired to the D input of the first flip-flop, the Q output of the first flip-flop is wired to the D input of the second flip-flop, and the Q output of the second flip-flop is the output "out".

diagram.alt: Two D flip-flops in series on one clock: in feeds the first, the first Q feeds the second D, and the second Q is out

solutionDiagram.alt: State graph of the two-bit shift register with self-loops at states 00 and 11

steps.title: What the state is and how a D flip-flop moves it
steps.body: The state of a sequential circuit is the tuple of its flip-flop outputs, and a state transition diagram has one node per state with an arrow for each input value. A positive edge-triggered D flip-flop copies its D input into Q at each rising clock edge: $Q^+ = D$. The two flip-flops are wired in series, so together they form a 2-bit shift register: the first takes "in", the second takes the first one's output. A self-loop is a transition from a state back to itself, and the question counts the states that have a self-loop for at least one value of "in".

steps.title: Next-state equations
steps.body: Write the state as $(A, B)$ with $A$ the output of the first flip-flop and $B$ the output of the second. Then the next state is $(A^+, B^+) = (\text{in}, A)$.

steps.title: Tabulate all four states
steps.body: State 00: in=0 gives 00, in=1 gives 10. State 01: in=0 gives 00, in=1 gives 10. State 10: in=0 gives 01, in=1 gives 11. State 11: in=0 gives 01, in=1 gives 11.

steps.title: Count self-loops
steps.body: A self-loop needs $(\text{in}, A) = (A, B)$, that is $A = \text{in}$ and $B = A$, so $A = B = \text{in}$. This holds for 00 with in=0 and for 11 with in=1, and for no other state (01 and 10 have $A \ne B$). So exactly 2 states have a transition back to themselves. The state graph shows the loops at 00 and 11.

shortcut.body: A self-loop in a shift register needs the incoming bit to equal what is already stored everywhere, so the register must be all 0s or all 1s: the answer is 2 for 2 flip-flops, and in general 2 for any number of stages. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: 4 counts every state, because each state has two outgoing arrows; but only the all-0 and all-1 states point back to themselves.
1 comes from checking only the all-zero state, which is the natural reset state; the state 11 also loops back when in=1.
3 or 0 come from mis-wiring the second flip-flop, for example taking $B^+ = \text{in}$, which gives every state a self-loop on one value of "in", or reading the clock as level-triggered.

recognize.clues: Two D flip-flops in series on one clock, with "in" feeding the first and the first output feeding the second: each edge shifts the stored bits along by one place.
recognize.contrast: A counter feeds back from its own outputs through gates, so a state moves along a fixed cycle; here the next state is set by the external input, so every state has two outgoing arrows.

check.body: Take a longer register of $n$ stages. A self-loop needs every stored bit to equal its left neighbour and the first bit to equal "in", so the whole register is constant. That gives 2 loop states for any $n$, and $n=2$ agrees with the count of 00 and 11. Directly: from 01 the input 0 goes to 00 and the input 1 goes to 10, so 01 never stays.

hints.text: What exactly is the "state" of this circuit, and what would a transition from a state back to itself require of the stored bits?
A positive edge-triggered D flip-flop copies its D input into its output at each rising edge, so each flip-flop simply passes along what it was given.
A state loops to itself when the new values of both flip-flops equal their old values. Write the new value of each flip-flop in terms of the old values and "in", then ask when new equals old.
Name the outputs $A$ and $B$, list the four combinations of $(A,B)$, and for each one try both values of "in" to see whether you land on the same pair.

variation.stem: Two positive edge-triggered D flip-flops share a clock. The input "in" drives $D_1$, and $D_2 = Q_1 + Q_2$ (an OR of both outputs). The state is $(Q_1, Q_2)$. The number of states of the state transition diagram that have a transition back to the same state for some value of "in" is _____.
variation.explanation: The next state is $(\text{in},\, Q_1+Q_2)$. A self-loop needs $Q_1=\text{in}$ and $Q_2=Q_1+Q_2$. The second condition holds when $Q_1=0$ (any $Q_2$) or when $Q_2=1$, which leaves the states 00, 01 and 11 (each with a suitable "in"). State 10 would move to 01 or 11, so it has no loop. The count is 3.

questions.stem: The next state table of a 2-bit saturating up-counter is given below. The counter is built as a synchronous sequential circuit using T flip-flops. The expressions for $T_1$ and $T_0$ are

solutionDiagram.alt: Saturating up-counter state chain 00, 01, 10, 11 with the T input values on each arrow

steps.title: The T flip-flop excitation rule
steps.body: A T flip-flop toggles when $T=1$ and holds when $T=0$, so $Q^+ = T\oplus Q$ and therefore $T = Q \oplus Q^+$: the input must be 1 exactly when the bit has to change. A saturating up-counter counts 00, 01, 10, 11 and then stays at 11 instead of wrapping to 00. To build it, find for every present state which bits change, which gives the required $T_1$ and $T_0$, and then write each as a Boolean function of $Q_1, Q_0$.

steps.title: Excitation table
steps.body: Compare each present state with its next state. 00 to 01: only $Q_0$ changes, $T_1T_0 = 01$. 01 to 10: both change, $T_1T_0 = 11$. 10 to 11: only $Q_0$ changes, $T_1T_0 = 01$. 11 to 11: nothing changes, $T_1T_0 = 00$.

steps.title: Read off the expressions
steps.body: $T_1 = 1$ only for $Q_1Q_0 = 01$, so $T_1 = \overline{Q_1}Q_0$. $T_0 = 0$ only for $Q_1Q_0 = 11$, so $T_0 = \overline{Q_1Q_0} = \overline{Q_1} + \overline{Q_0}$. This is option (B). The other options contradict the table: (A) has $T_1 = 0$ at 01, (C) has $T_1 = 1$ at 11 and (D) has $T_0 = 0$ at 00.

shortcut.body: Only two entries of the table are special: $T_1$ is 1 in one row (01) and $T_0$ is 0 in one row (11). So $T_1 = \overline{Q_1}Q_0$ and $T_0 = \overline{Q_1Q_0}$. Or test rows on the options: at 00 the required $T_1T_0$ is 01, which removes D ($T_0=Q_1+Q_0=0$); at 01 it is 11, which removes A ($T_1=Q_1Q_0=0$); at 11 it is 00, which removes C ($T_1=Q_1+Q_0=1$). About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Option A has $T_1 = Q_1Q_0$, which is 1 at 11 (where the counter must hold) and 0 at 01 (where $Q_1$ must flip); $T_0 = \overline{Q_1}\,\overline{Q_0}$ is 1 only at 00 and misses 01 and 10.
Option C has $T_1 = Q_1 + Q_0$, which is 1 at 11 and 10, so $Q_1$ toggles there; at 11 it would clear $Q_1$ instead of saturating.
Option D has the correct $T_1$ but $T_0 = Q_1 + Q_0$, which is 0 at 00 where $Q_0$ must toggle to 1, and 1 at 11 where it must hold. A candidate who drops the complements swaps these cases.

recognize.clues: A next-state table is given and the circuit must be built from T flip-flops, so the task is to find the input each flip-flop needs for every listed transition.
recognize.contrast: Reading a given circuit forwards (circuit analysis) goes from inputs to next state; here you go backwards from the wanted next state to the inputs, which is what an excitation table is for.

check.body: Substitute each row into the chosen expressions and confirm $Q^+ = T\oplus Q$. At 01: $T_1 = 1\cdot 1 = 1$ and $T_0 = 1$, so $Q_1^+ = 0\oplus 1 = 1$ and $Q_0^+ = 1\oplus 1 = 0$, which is 10 as the table says. At 11: $T_1 = 0$ and $T_0 = 0$, so the state holds at 11.

A T flip-flop holds its value when $T=0$ and toggles when $T=1$, so $Q^+ = T \oplus Q$.

Compare $Q_1$ with $Q_1^+$ and $Q_0$ with $Q_0^+$ row by row to fill a column for $T_1$ and one for $T_0$, then express each column as a Boolean function of $Q_1, Q_0$.

variation.stem: A 2-bit saturating down-counter steps 11, 10, 01, 00 and then stays at 00. It is built as a synchronous circuit with T flip-flops. Which option gives $T_1$ and $T_0$?
variation.explanation: $T$ is 1 exactly where a bit changes. The steps 11 to 10, 10 to 01, 01 to 00 and 00 to 00 give $T_1T_0$ = 01, 11, 01 and 00. So $T_1$ is 1 only at 10, giving $Q_1\overline{Q_0}$, and $T_0$ is 0 only at 00, giving $Q_1+Q_0$. Option B is the up-counter answer, and option D keeps $T_0$ wrong at 01 and 10.

questions.stem: Consider a combination of T and D flip-flops connected as shown below. The output of the D flip-flop is connected to the input of the T flip-flop and the output of the T flip-flop is connected to the input of the D flip-flop. Initially, both $Q_0$ and $Q_1$ are set to 1 (before the 1st clock cycle). The outputs
questions.figure: A T flip-flop with output Q1 and a D flip-flop with output Q0 share one clock. The Q1 output is wired to the D input of the D flip-flop. The Q0 output is wired back to the T input of the T flip-flop, closing the loop.
options: $Q_1Q_0$ after the 3rd cycle are 11 and after the 4th cycle are 00 respectively
$Q_1Q_0$ after the 3rd cycle are 11 and after the 4th cycle are 01 respectively
$Q_1Q_0$ after the 3rd cycle are 00 and after the 4th cycle are 11 respectively
$Q_1Q_0$ after the 3rd cycle are 01 and after the 4th cycle are 01 respectively

diagram.alt: A T flip-flop whose output Q1 feeds a D flip-flop and whose T input is fed by the D flip-flop output Q0, on one clock

solutionDiagram.alt: State graph of Q1Q0: the cycle 11, 01, 10 with the transitions labelled by clock number

steps.title: The two flip-flop rules
steps.body: A T flip-flop toggles when its input $T$ is 1 and holds when it is 0: $Q^+ = T\oplus Q$. A D flip-flop copies its input: $Q^+ = D$. Both flip-flops share one clock, so at each clock edge both are updated together, each from the values just before the edge. Following the wiring: the T flip-flop has output $Q_1$ and its input is $Q_0$; the D flip-flop has output $Q_0$ and its input is $Q_1$.

steps.title: Next-state equations
steps.body: $Q_1^+ = Q_1 \oplus Q_0$ (the T input is $Q_0$) and $Q_0^+ = Q_1$ (the D input is $Q_1$). The new $Q_0$ is the old $Q_1$, not the new one: the flip-flops do not ripple within one clock.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: After the 3rd cycle $Q_1Q_0 = 11$, and after the 4th cycle $Q_1Q_0 = 01$. That is option (B). The sequence 11, 01, 10 repeats every 3 clocks (see the state graph), so the state after clock 4 equals the state after clock 1.

shortcut.body: The states cycle with period 3 (11, 01, 10), so after clock 3 you are back at 11 and after clock 4 at 01. Option B is the only one with 11 then 01, and checking just these two states takes about a minute.

traps.text: Option A (11 then 00) comes from letting $Q_0$ take the new $Q_1$ in the same clock, a ripple view. In a synchronous circuit the D flip-flop sees the old $Q_1$, so the state after clock 4 is 01.
Option C (00 then 11) has the machine in state 00 after the 3rd clock; 00 never occurs from 11, because the only state that leads into 00 is 00 itself.
Option D (01 then 01) gives the state after the 1st clock for the 3rd cycle: a candidate who counts the initial state as cycle 1 is off by one or two clocks.

recognize.clues: A T flip-flop and a D flip-flop are wired into each other on a shared clock with a stated starting state, and the question asks for the outputs after the 3rd and 4th cycle: trace the circuit clock by clock.
recognize.contrast: A ripple counter clocks each stage from the previous output, so changes cascade; here one clock drives both flip-flops, so every update uses the old values.

check.body: The map $(Q_1,Q_0)\mapsto(Q_1\oplus Q_0,\,Q_1)$ sends 11 to 01, 01 to 10 and 10 to 11, so the three states form a cycle of length 3. Clock 4 equals clock 1 (4 mod 3 = 1), which gives 01, and clock 3 returns to 11. State 00 maps to itself, so it is unreachable from 11.

variation.explanation: The next state is $(Q_1\oplus Q_0,\, Q_1)$, built from the old values. From 01 the clocks give 10, 11, 01, 10, 11, so the 4th cycle gives 10 and the 5th gives 11. The sequence repeats every 3 clocks, so clock 5 equals clock 2. Option B puts the 5th state at 01, which is the state after clock 3.
